messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mele had spent most of her adult life building a reputation as a careful, exacting auditor, someone who could sit with ledgers and discrepancies for hours without losing the thread. Now, at seventy-five, she still worked part-time, preferring the order of her office to the looser rhythms of retirement. She was a married woman from a Pacific Island family who had lived in the United States for many years, but the event that divided her life had happened much earlier, when she was a civilian in a war zone. She rarely managed to tell it straight through. What came instead were fragments: a cramped room packed with frightened people, the sour press of sweat and unwashed bodies, the sense that danger was moving just outside, and sudden still images of faces and walls as if the worst moments had been stored as photographs rather than a story. When she tried to describe what happened, she would stop, shake her head, and say she knew exactly what had happened but could not find words for it.

Over the years, certain moments began to pull those fragments back with unusual force. The smell of body odour on a crowded elevator or in the hallway outside her office could make her feel as if the air had changed and the war had returned with it; when that happened, she did not merely remember in an ordinary way but could actually smell again what she had smelled then. The workplace itself had become charged. If a colleague passed too close after hurrying up the stairs, or if she caught the mixed scent of wool, old paper, and perspiration in a conference room, the images came at her as stark visual flashes. Strangest to her, feeling briefly happy or relaxed could do the same. A quiet dinner with her husband or an easy afternoon balancing accounts might be interrupted by the thought that calm was dangerous, and in that instant the old images broke in. Those moments also carried a stab of meaning: she had come to believe that if she could be jolted out of peace so quickly, then something about the war was still visible on her, as though other people could look at her and see exactly what had happened.

That belief deepened each time the memories forced themselves forward. The more vividly she smelled the bodies and saw those frozen scenes, the more convinced she became that the damage was permanent. What frightened her most was not only the memory itself but what it seemed to prove—that she would never feel normal emotions again, that even happiness was suspect, and that a life like this might not be worth much. At times she sat in session looking composed and professionally dressed, yet speaking in the flat, resigned way of someone who had begun to take these conclusions as facts.

Once she had come to see herself in that way, she moved through the world as if exposed and unsafe. In restaurants and at work she insisted on taking the chair with her back to the wall so she could see the room. Walking from the parking lot into the office, she repeatedly checked behind her to make sure no one was following. There were also moments of reckless indifference that unsettled her husband—crossing a street too quickly, driving when overtired, acting as if harm no longer mattered much. These habits were not random to her; if people could see what had happened to her, and if normal feeling was gone for good, then vigilance felt like the only sensible position.

The vigilance fed the problem it was trying to contain. Scanning every room, keeping her body braced, and looking over her shoulder sharpened her sense of danger until the old scenes arrived again with photographic clarity. A stranger’s sweat on the train into work, noticed because she was already on alert, could bring back the smell of that room in the war within seconds. Afterward she would spend hours ruminating: going over how the event might have been prevented, turning repeatedly to why it had happened to her, as if enough mental effort could finally produce an explanation that would settle her. Before even ordinary interactions with coworkers, she rehearsed what she would say, determined not to betray herself. Yet these efforts left her more entangled in the trauma. The repeated mental review made the sensory fragments more available, not less, and the more she searched for meaning the more she landed on the same punishing conclusions—that she was marked, emptied out, beyond repair. From there she became still more guarded and watchful.

By the time she sought help, the loop had tightened around daily life. Her office, once a place of competence, had become one of the main places she felt ambushed by smell, by proximity, by brief moments of ease that turned instantly into alarm. Her husband had urged her to come after noticing how often she positioned herself to monitor a room and how little pleasure she seemed able to trust. Mele said she was not coming because she believed talking would be easy; she still could not find words for much of what happened. She came because she was tired of living as if danger were always one breath away, and because part of her, despite everything, still hoped it might be possible to feel something other than dread without being punished for it.
